subject: spinning space capsule
title: What If Your Spacecraft Spun Once a Second? Armstrong Lived It in 1966

scenes.text: What if your capsule started spinning once a second and wouldn't stop? Neil Armstrong found out.
March 16, 1966. Gemini 8 had just made the first docking in space, with an Agena rocket stage. Twenty-seven minutes later, the pair began to roll.
Armstrong undocked. The roll got worse: a thruster had short-circuited and was stuck firing. The capsule hit about one revolution per second.
At that rate you black out. Two men, seconds from passing out over the Pacific, out of anyone's reach.
Armstrong cut the main thrusters and fired the re-entry jets, meant only for landing. The spin stopped. It had burned 75 percent of that fuel.
Rules said: land now. Three days became ten hours and 41 minutes, and a splashdown near Okinawa. Three years later, he walked on the Moon.

description:
What if your spacecraft began spinning once every second? On 16 March 1966, 27 minutes after Gemini 8 made the first docking in space, a short-circuited thruster stuck open and the capsule rolled up to about one revolution per second, close to the point where the crew would black out.
Neil Armstrong shut down the main thrusters and used the re-entry control system to stop the spin, burning 75 percent of its fuel, which under NASA's rules forced an immediate landing: a planned three-day mission ended after 10 hours 41 minutes with a splashdown about 800 kilometres from Okinawa.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: The crew then bobbed in the Pacific for three hours before the recovery ship reached them. Which space emergency should we run through next?
